storm.summary_layperson: A cluster of strong thunderstorms tracking up from the New York City area is likely to reach the cove around 11 PM, and with the Sound's usual protective effects already gone for the night, it should arrive close to full strength.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Neither the sea breeze (collapsed by about 7:30 PM) nor the marine layer (air-water gap already down to about 4°F, under the ~5°F protective threshold by 9 PM) is left to blunt tonight's storms — no local buffer for this window.
storm.detail_html:
Radar out of KOKX shows a line of strong storms (max reflectivity 48 dBZ) tracking ENE at roughly 32 kt, currently about 44 miles southwest of the cove near the NYC metro. High instability (CAPE 3200 J/kg) and 22 kt of 0–6 km shear back up the NWS Area Forecast Discussion's read of a continuing strong-to-severe wind threat overnight, particularly for areas north and west of the city.

For the 22:00–03:00 window, both of the cove's usual local defenses are down. The sea breeze died around 7:34 PM, more than two hours before this window opens, so any wind through the night is gradient-only, not thermal. The marine layer — the stable, cool air layer that forms when the Sound is colder than the air above it and can choke incoming storms — is gone too: the air-water gap had already dropped to about 4°F by 9 PM, under the ~5°F threshold this pipeline treats as "on," and keeps falling toward near-zero by early morning. Neither mechanism will meaningfully weaken tonight's storms.

The nearest tracked cell is projected to reach the cove around 10:57 PM, with high confidence from a clean two-scan radar motion fix (32 kt ENE), inside a window of roughly 10:39–11:15 PM. Because neither local discount applies, that window carries no late-edge stretch — it's the raw radar-motion ETA, unadjusted. With CAPE still around 3200 J/kg, favor the early edge of the window for punch-through-style intensification rather than the late edge.

Compared with nearby coastal towns that don't get any benefit from the Sound's crossing geometry, the cove isn't catching a special break tonight — this storm should hit here about as hard as it hits Rye or New Rochelle. If the cell weakens or slows on radar before 10:30 PM, that would be reason to soften this call.

A Heat Advisory remains in effect through 8 PM Friday and a regional Air Quality Alert is active — neither bears on the storm risk directly, but both are live NWS products worth flagging for anyone out overnight.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 42 mi SW closing at 30 kt, arriving after both the sea breeze and the marine layer have already faded for the night — expect it close to full strength.

wind.tactics_blurb: Wind is light (2–4 kt) and swings through nearly every quadrant overnight with no sea breeze to anchor it — no side of the course holds a consistent edge. Watch for a brief squally shift near 11 PM as a tracked storm cell closes from the SW.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a post-thermal window: sunset was 8:04 PM and the sea breeze had already collapsed around 7:34 PM, roughly 2.5 hours before 22:00. The land-sea temperature contrast that drives the sea breeze (deltaT, the air-water temperature difference) peaked at only 4.1°F today — under the ~5°F gate needed to sustain a sea breeze into the evening in the first place, so there's no thermal signature to track through this window.

What's left is background gradient flow, and HRRR shows it as very light — 2 to 4 kt — and directionless: the hour-by-hour forecast swings from SW (219°) at 10 PM to NNE (29°) at 11 PM to ESE (114°) at midnight to SSW (205°) at 1 AM to W (263°) at 2 AM and back to SW (228°) at 3 AM. That's not a coherent shift pattern; it's the model resolving near-calm flow where small pressure perturbations dominate rather than any organized regime. Station agreement backs this up — direction agreement across the surface network sits at just 0.43, and the observed wind at Riverside YC itself is a barely-there 0.9 kt out of the E.

With no sea breeze and no steady gradient, no side of the cove holds a consistent pressure or lift advantage tonight — this is a hold-center, don't-commit night rather than a play-the-shore night.

The one wrinkle: a radar-tracked storm cell is projected to reach the cove around 10:57 PM (see the storm section), which falls inside the 23:00 hour of this table. Convective outflow ahead of and during that cell's passage can produce a brief, sharp wind shift and gusts well above the ambient 2–4 kt shown here — the HRRR background field doesn't capture that. Treat the 23:00 row as the ambient forecast only; expect it to be interrupted around 11 PM.

Confidence in the direction calls is low across the board — the sea-breeze correction block flags "low" direction confidence even at fetch time — which is normal for light-and-variable overnight flow. Don't read precision into any single hour's compass point.
